newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire says Mobutu-Kabila talks imminent to end war.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says Mobutu-Kabila talks imminent to end war.

text.p: Zaire's embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila could meet shortly after negotiations between their envoys, Zaire Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba said on Wednesday.
Such a meeting would send a sigh of relief in the Zaire capital where fear of enchroaching rebel war is growing.
"Things are getting clearer. Plans are afoot for a meeting between the head of state and the rebel leader. This meeting is imminent," Kin-Kiey told a news conference in Kinshasa.

Kin-Kiey spoke shortly after Kabila arrived in South Africa, where envoys of the veteran president and the guerrilla leader have held talks over the past few weeks. Kabila himself was in South Africa last month.

Kabila held talks with South African President Nelson Mandela on Wednesday evening in Cape Town where a government source said a meeting between Mobutu and the rebel leader could talk place as soon as this weekend.
Kabila's rebels have seized half the country in the six-month-old civil war and are now targeting Kinshasa, the remaining bastion of the ailing Mobutu.
"I believe Kabila went to South Africa to take charge of the negotiations," Kin-Kiey said, adding Togo, Congo and South Africa itself had volunteered to host the meeting.
Earlier Kabila appeared to dampen hopes for averting war in the teeming capital of five million people by rejecting any truce in his whirlwind armed campaign to topple Mobutu.
Western military analysts in Kinshasa say the rebels have moved further on from their last conquest, Kananga, in West Kasai Province, which they seized last Saturday.

One analyst placed the guerrillas around Tshikapa, a diamond trading centre close to the Angolan border and on the highway to the town of Kikwit, in Zaire's Bandundu Province some 350 km (200 miles) from Kinshasa.
At the same time, Mobutu's opponents in the capital considered further plans to disrupt normal life in the city, making the prospect of a rebel takeover that much easier.
Before leaving for South Africa from Zaire's second city Lubumbashi, Kabila again asserted that nothing would halt his drive to unseat Mobutu.
"There will be no ceasefire until Mobutu relinquishes power," the rebel leader said.
Kabila has long demanded direct talks with Mobutu but he says these should only serve to define Mobutu's resignation.
Kabila's firm rejection of a ceasefire heightened international concern about the likelihood of tragedy in Kinshasa should rebel forces reach the capital.
After crippling Kinshasa with anti-Mobutu protest action on Monday and Tuesday, Zaire's main opposition called a meeting of its leadership on Wednesday to plan further measures.
"We will launch new measures for the coming week. The action will continue," declared Mukendi wa Mulumba, chief political aide to opposition stalwart Etienne Tshisekedi.

Shops and businesses reopened on Wednesday and the city regained its normal rhythm after a well-observed stay-at-home protest on Monday. Police thwarted a student protest march on Tuesday but Kinshasa residents stayed at home all the same.

Opposition spokesman Laurent Mbayo said Mobutu had agreed to talks after being humiliated by the rebels, who gave him a three-day ultimatum to step down by last Sunday. The rebels resumed their military advances on Monday.
"He was given an ultimatum. It's the only language he understands. He was humiliated and that's why he reacted," Mbayo told Reuters.
